What a queue gets you that a scheduled job never will

The scheduled job is the first thing everybody reaches for, and it is right often
enough to be a habit. The habit survives well past the point where it stops being right, because
the failure it produces is invisible.
The three ways it fails quietly

The job takes longer than its interval, so a second copy starts while the first is running.
    Now two of them are working on the same rows. Whether that is harmless or catastrophic depends
    on code that was written assuming it could never happen.

The other common guard is a lock file: if the previous run is still going, do nothing. That is
    safer and it means a slow run swallows the next one, with nothing anywhere saying so.
It has no idea what is in it

A scheduled job knows the time. It does not know that one particular item has failed on eleven
    consecutive runs, because it has no concept of an item at all.

The third one is the expensive failure. Everything looks healthy — the job runs, exits zero,
  logs nothing alarming — and one record has been silently failing since March.
Not a message broker. Not infrastructure. A table:

create table work (
  id          bigserial primary key,
  kind        text        not null,
  payload     jsonb       not null,
  state       text        not null default 'ready',   -- ready | running | done | failed
  attempts    int         not null default 0,
  run_after   timestamptz not null default now(),
  last_error  text,
  updated_at  timestamptz not null default now()
);
And one query that takes the next item without two workers taking the same one:

update work set state = 'running', attempts = attempts + 1, updated_at = now()
where id = (
  select id from work
  where state = 'ready' and run_after <= now()
  order by run_after
  for update skip locked          -- the whole trick is on this line
  limit 1
)
returning *;
-- the whole trick is on this line

is what makes this safe with several workers: each one
  takes a row nobody else has locked, rather than queueing behind the same row. It has been in
  PostgreSQL since 9.5 and it removes the only genuinely hard part of writing a queue.
What you get for those thirty lines

The retry column is the one that changes daily life. With a scheduled job, fixing one bad record
means running the whole batch again and hoping the rest is idempotent. With a queue it is one
update.
A scheduled job knows what time it is. A queue knows what is wrong.

None of this removes the timer — something still has to wake up and put work into the queue, and a
scheduled job is the right tool for exactly that. The change is what it does when it wakes: it
enqueues, and something else does the work.
That split is the whole idea, and it is why this is a small change rather than a migration.

Do I need a message broker for this?

No. A table with a state column and one query using `for update skip locked` gives you safe concurrent workers, retries and per-item visibility. A broker earns its place at volumes and durability guarantees most internal systems never reach.
What stops two workers taking the same job?

`for update skip locked` in the claiming query. Each worker locks a row nobody else has locked instead of queueing behind the same one. It has been in PostgreSQL since 9.5 and it removes the only genuinely hard part of writing a queue.
Do I still need a scheduled job?

Yes, and that is the point. Something has to wake up and put work into the queue, and a timer is exactly right for that. What changes is that it enqueues rather than does the work, so a slow item no longer blocks the next run.
How do I stop an item retrying forever?

Cap the attempts and move the row to a failed state when it is exceeded. Then the important half: something has to look at that state. A failed queue nobody reads is the same silence you left the scheduled job to escape, only with better bookkeeping.

Anywhere that can reach the database. A long-running process, a container, or a scheduled job that drains the queue for a minute and exits — all three work, because the queue holds the state rather than the worker. That is what makes them replaceable without anything being lost.
A job that runs every hour hides its failures for an hour, overlaps with itself under load, and cannot tell you which item is stuck. A queue is barely more code.
A scheduled job fails quietly in three ways: it overlaps itself, silently skips, or hides a single stuck item.
A queue is one table and one query — the whole trick is `for update skip locked`.
What you gain is per-item state: what is stuck, how far behind you are, and retrying one record instead of all of them.
Keep the timer. Its job becomes putting work into the queue rather than doing the work.

Serverless is a billing model, not an architecture

Everybody argues about serverless as though it were an architecture. It is not. It
is a way of being charged, and almost every real consequence — good and bad — follows from that
one fact rather than from anything technical.

A server you rent costs the same whether it serves ten requests a day or ten thousand. A function
you deploy costs nothing until it runs. That is the entire difference, and it is a big one, but it
is a difference on the invoice.
Once you see it that way, the arguments sort themselves out.
What the billing model gives you

If your traffic is spiky, bursty, or mostly nothing, you stop paying for the gaps. A contact form
that gets fourteen submissions a week does not need a machine standing by all week. Neither does a
webhook receiver, a scheduled report, or the little service that resizes an image when somebody
uploads one.

The clearest win is the thing that runs rarely and must not be forgotten. Nobody wants to
  maintain a virtual machine whose entire job is to receive a form four times a day — and nobody
  does maintain it, which is how you end up with an unpatched box on the internet.

The second gift is that you stop operating a machine. No package updates, no disk filling up, no
certificate expiring at two in the morning. That work does not disappear, but it moves to somebody
whose full-time job it is.
You cannot keep anything in memory

A function may run in a fresh instance every time. Anything you want to remember has to be
    written somewhere that outlives the request, and that store is now a second thing to pay for,
    secure and reason about.

Every platform caps how long one invocation may run. Work that takes minutes has to be cut
    into pieces that hand off to each other, which is a real design cost and the usual reason a
    serverless project turns miserable.

The emulators are good and they are still emulators. The gap between "works on my machine" and
    "works deployed" is wider here than with a container you can run identically in both places.

Paying nothing at idle is the same property as paying without limit under load. A loop that
    calls itself, or a scraper that finds you, is a bill rather than a crash — and a crash is much
    easier to notice.
The useful question is not "serverless or not". It is:

does this thing spend most of its life
doing nothing?
Idle almost always; each run is milliseconds
Runs briefly, then nothing for a day
API in front of a database
Connection pooling is the whole problem — see below
The model charges for time; long connections are all time
A rented machine is cheaper and simpler at that point

The "maybe" row is where most people get hurt. A traditional database expects a handful of
long-lived connections; a serverless platform can hand it hundreds of short ones at once, and the
database falls over long before your function does. Every platform now has an answer — a proxy, a
pooler, an HTTP-speaking database — and every one of those answers is another piece to run.

Paying nothing at idle and paying without limit under load are the same property,
seen from two sides.

Serverless is excellent for the long tail of small things every organisation accumulates: the
form, the hook, the nightly job, the glue. It is a poor fit for the one busy thing at the centre,
which is exactly the thing people are most tempted to move first because it is the most expensive.
Start at the edges. Leave the middle alone until something forces you.
Is serverless cheaper than a virtual machine?

Only when the work is idle most of the time. A function that runs a few thousand times a month costs practically nothing, while a machine costs the same whether it works or not. Under steady all-day load the rented machine wins, and usually by a wide margin.
What happens if something calls my function in a loop?

You get an invoice rather than an outage, which is harder to notice. Every platform lets you cap spending or requests per day — set that limit on the first day, before there is anything worth attacking, because the default is unlimited.
Can I run a normal database behind serverless functions?

Yes, but connection pooling becomes the whole problem. Traditional databases expect a few long-lived connections and a serverless platform hands them hundreds of short ones. Use the platform's pooler or a database that speaks HTTP, and treat that extra piece as part of the cost.

Much less than they did, and it depends entirely on the runtime. Platforms built on lightweight isolates start in single-digit milliseconds; container-based ones can still stall on the first request after a quiet period. If a delay of a second occasionally would hurt, measure it on your platform before designing around it.
Is serverless the same thing as edge?

No, though the same products often sell both. Serverless is about how you are charged and how instances appear; edge is about where the code runs geographically. A function can be serverless and run in one region, or run in fifty and be billed by the hour.
The interesting property was never "no servers". It is that idle costs nothing — and every design consequence follows from that one line on the invoice.
Serverless changes what you are charged for, not how the system is built: you pay per run instead of per hour.
That makes it excellent for anything that is idle most of the time — forms, webhooks, nightly jobs.
It is a poor fit for steady all-day load, long connections, or work that will not finish inside one invocation.
Paying nothing at idle and paying without limit under load are the same property, so put a cap on the account.

It works and it is faster to set up. In exchange a third party holds your messages, shows its branding, sets your rate limits and changes its pricing without asking. For roughly forty lines you keep all of that, and the messages go wherever you want.

It stops the cheap kind. A hidden field that only a bot fills in, a minimum message length and a per-address rate limit remove most automated noise. A determined human is a different problem, and no form handler solves that one.

Where should the messages actually go?

Wherever you will read them. A spreadsheet works and is easy to share; a mailbox works and needs no login; a database is right once you need to search them. The function hides that choice, so changing your mind later costs one deployment and no edit to the form.

The question is not whether it is a serious platform. It is whether the thing you
are building will ever need one.

Most small internal tools never do. The ones that do usually announce it clearly — a quota you
keep hitting, a run that will not fit in the time limit — and by then you know enough about the
problem to rebuild it properly in a fortnight.
Is Apps Script safe to expose to the internet?

Not directly. Put an edge function in front of it: the script's address stays private, validation and rate limiting happen before any quota is spent, and you avoid the awkward cross-origin behaviour of published web apps. Calling it server to server sidesteps that entirely.

A per-execution runtime cap of a few minutes, plus daily quotas on mail and total script runtime. The exact numbers differ by account type and change over time, so check the current figures before designing against them rather than trusting any article, including this one.
When should I move off it?

When you keep hitting a quota, when a job will not fit inside the execution limit, or when you are still extending the thing in a year. Any of those three is the platform telling you the problem outgrew it, and by then you understand the problem well enough to rebuild it quickly.
Can I keep the code in version control?

Yes, and it is the first thing to set up. Google's command-line tool pushes and pulls the project so the source lives in git like anything else. Editing production code in a browser tab, with no history and no review, is exactly as bad as it sounds.

The only query optimisation that always works is reading less

Tuning almost always starts in the wrong place — at the settings, the machine, the
engine — and almost always ends in the same place: something was reading far more data than the
answer needed.

Everything below is a way of reading less. There is no sixth idea, and there is no setting that
makes reading a hundred gigabytes fast.
On a columnar store — which is what every analytical warehouse is —

is not a
convenience, it is a bill. The engine reads only the columns you name, so naming all of them costs
exactly as much as it sounds like it should.

Rows are stored together, so reading one column still reads the whole row off disk. Selecting
    fewer columns saves transfer, not much else.

Each column is stored separately. Naming three columns out of ninety reads three ninetieths of
    the data, and the difference is not subtle.
The same query has completely different economics depending on the layout underneath.

A partitioned table is split into pieces by some column — nearly always a date. If the query says
which piece it wants, the engine never opens the others.

-- Reads every partition: the function hides the column from the planner
where date_trunc('day', created_at) = '2026-05-01'

-- Reads one: the column is compared directly to a constant range
where created_at >= '2026-05-01' and created_at < '2026-05-02'
-- Reads every partition: the function hides the column from the planner
-- Reads one: the column is compared directly to a constant range

Wrapping the partition column in a function is the single most common way people lose
  partition pruning without noticing. The query is still correct, still returns the same rows, and
  now reads the whole table. Nothing warns you.
Read fewer blocks within a partition

Clustering — sorting the data physically by a column you filter on — lets the engine skip blocks
inside a partition. It is the cheapest big win available, because it changes nothing about how the
data is queried.

Read fewer rows before the join
Joins multiply. Filtering after a join means the engine built rows it was about to throw away.

Push every condition as close to the source table as it will go. Modern planners do a lot of
    this for you, and they stop being able to as soon as the query gets complicated enough for it
    to matter.
Aggregate before joining, where you can
Joining two tables of a million rows to then count them is a very expensive way to count.

Why did my query get slower after I added a date filter?

Almost always because the filter wraps the partition column in a function, which hides it from the planner. The query stays correct and quietly reads every partition. Compare the column directly against a range instead, and nothing will warn you if you do not.
Should I cluster on the column I group by?

No — cluster on what you filter by. Clustering lets the engine skip blocks it does not need to open, and it can only skip based on the filter. Clustering on a reporting dimension is the most common way to do this work and gain nothing.
Is a bigger machine ever the right answer?

Sometimes, as a deliberate stopgap while you fix the query. It works once, the problem returns at the new size, and the invoice stays larger permanently. Treat it as buying time rather than as a fix, and write down what you bought the time for.
Will adding an index fix this?

On a row store, often yes — an index is precisely a way to read fewer rows. On a columnar warehouse there are usually no indexes at all, and partitioning and clustering do that job instead. Knowing which kind of store you are on decides which half of this advice applies.
How do I find out what a query really read?

Every engine will tell you: the execution plan, plus the bytes or rows scanned. Read that number before and after each change, because it is the thing you are actually optimising. Wall-clock time moves for reasons that have nothing to do with your query.
Most slow queries are not slow because the engine is slow. They are slow because they read a year to answer a question about a week, and no amount of tuning fixes that.
Most slow queries read far more data than the answer needs; no setting fixes that.
Name your columns, keep partition pruning by never wrapping the date column in a function.
Cluster on what you filter by, not what you group by, and filter before joining rather than after.
